newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Thousands demand return to Communism in Crimea.
newsitem.headline: Thousands demand return to Communism in Crimea.

text.p: Thousands of people demanded a return to communist power in Ukraine's southern peninsula of Crimea on Tuesday, during a nationwide leftist "Day of Action" against unpaid wages in the former Soviet republic.
"Power to the communists!" the crowd of about 3,500 chanted, waving a sea of red flags and banners with slogans like "The motherland is calling you back to the USSR."
"We demand the state immediately change its social-economic and political course," another slogan read.
Left-wing groups had tried to organise a national strike and communist deputies quit the chamber in the capital Kiev in protest over a backlog of unpaid wages and pensions.
But a coal-mining official told Reuters by telephone from Donetsk, centre of the eastern mining region, that only eight of 250 pits were on strike -- "about the same number as usual".
The non-payments mountain, put at 4.2 billion hryvnias by President Leonid Kuchma recently, is growing all the time as parliament has yet to pass a 1997 budget.
Elsewhere smaller crowds gathered in the streets to register their protest at average monthly wages of $80 to $90, pensions of $30 and price growth of almost 40 percent last year.
The coal mining official said only 200 communists had gathered on the central square of Donetsk.
Communists were due to rally later in Kiev -- but about 500 nationalists who broadly back reforms and President Leonid Kuchma beat them to it with a morning rally outside parliament.

"Communist pigs! Filth!" yelled one elderly woman, giving voice to hatred for the memory of the Soviet-era Communist Party whose successor occupies 90 of 420 seats -- the biggest single group in parliament.
Some of the crowd of supporters of the nationalist Rukh party, which spearheaded Ukraine's independence drive in 1991, blew whistles with blue and yellow nationalist ribbons.
They blamed the non-payments on the fact that so many members of Ukraine's industrialist class are former communists.
"Tell me where I can find a Rukh member running a state enterprise?" asked Mykhailo Zebensky, a protester in his 30s.
"In Ukraine 80 percent of the factory bosses are communists. They're the ones who are not paying wages. They've re-painted themselves. They're still communists underneath," he said.
The crowds in Simferopol were boosted by pro-Moscow sentiment in the peninsula, where 75 percent of the population is ethnic Russian and many want a return to Kremlin rule.
"Kuchma! Don't scare us with NATO! We want a union with our Russian brother!" one banner read.
Ukraine has not ruled out seeking entry to the Western military alliance in future but the communists were more interested in joining forces with like-minded kin in Russia.
